title: Choosing between them, and the honest answer that it should stay relational

videos.script: This course has spent twenty-one lessons on three databases that are not relational. This last one says when you should use none of them. {{none}} The question usually arrives as a brand. MongoDB or Cassandra? It has no answer in that form. The question that has one is about operations. What is read, what is written, and what it costs when two copies disagree. {{table}} Then we run Postgres beside the other three. A document column with an index that answers containment. An upsert that counts. A cache table that empties itself after a crash. A queue where two workers never take the same job. {{postgres}} Postgres has real limits, and we name them. Writes across many machines. Writes in two regions at once. Structures at memory speed. {{limits}} When one of those is real, adding a second database is right. And it costs something. Two backups. Two skills on call. And a write that reaches one database and not the other. {{dual}} The fix is an outbox. Last, you write the choice down, so the next person knows why. For most of the shop, the answer stays relational.
